**Reading map:** Deisenroth, Faisal & Ong, *Mathematics for Machine Learning* (2020), Chapter 11 §11.4. All examples are newly authored.

## Motivation

The mixture becomes clearer if we introduce an unobserved category Z indicating which component generated an order time. We integrate Z out because we never directly observe it.

## Derivation and notation

$$
Z\sim\mathrm{Categorical}(\boldsymbol\pi),\quad T\mid Z=k\sim\mathcal N(\mu_k,\sigma_k^2),\quad p(t)=\sum_k p(t,Z=k)
$$

Read this model together with the distributional, geometric or optimisation assumptions. An equation without its domain of validity is not a complete explanation.

## Apply it to our running example

A synthetic order first samples a regime Z, then samples a time from that regime's Gaussian. Observing only T=18 does not reveal Z with certainty; Bayes' rule yields a posterior distribution over possible regimes.

## Constraints and interpretation

Soft assignments differ from hard clustering. Hidden components are statistical devices; causally identifying a real 'local vs long' operating regime requires separate domain evidence.

## Your turn

If both components have identical means and variances, can an observed time reveal which component generated it?
